title: Crisis Leadership
description: Leading through outages, security incidents, reputational risk, layoffs, or customer-trust events with calm execution and clear communication.

competency.name: Crisis Leadership
competency.definition: Maintains clarity, decision quality, communication, and learning when stakes and uncertainty are high.
competency.whyItMatters: Senior leaders are often most visible when systems fail, trust is strained, or the organization is under pressure.

prompt.primary: Tell me about the most serious production incident you led through.
variants: Describe a time when you had to communicate bad technical news to customers or executives.
Tell me about a time you led through a security, reputational, or organizational crisis.
interviewerIntent: Can the candidate stay calm and structured?
Do they separate **incident command**, stakeholder communication, and recovery?
Does the crisis lead to rigorous learning rather than blame?

scenario.signatureExample: During a major outage, the CTO separates incident command from **executive communication** and later changes architecture, ownership, and alerting.
context: A critical service outage affects major customers.
Executives need updates while engineers need focus.
The **root cause** is unclear during the first hour.
constraints: Communication must be frequent but not speculative.
The review must be blameless but rigorous.

storyAnatomy.situation: A major customer-facing outage created pressure from customers, executives, and internal teams.
storyAnatomy.task: Restore service, communicate clearly, and make sure the organization learned the right lessons.
action: Established an incident commander and kept executives out of the troubleshooting path.
Created a separate communication channel for customers and executives.
Tracked decisions, hypotheses, and recovery criteria.
Led a **post-incident** review that focused on architecture, ownership, monitoring, and escalation.
result: The team restored service with less coordination noise.
Follow-up work reduced recurrence risk and improved detection.
storyAnatomy.reflection: The lesson was that calm crisis leadership is mostly about reducing ambiguity and protecting attention.

exampleStories.title: Major Customer Outage
exampleStories.promptVariant: Tell me about the most serious production incident you led through.
exampleStories.situation: A critical service outage affected top customers while engineers were still unsure whether the trigger was deployment, dependency saturation, or data corruption.
strongAnswerSketch: Assign **incident command** and keep troubleshooting channels focused.
Create a separate executive/customer update rhythm with facts, unknowns, and next update time.
Make **recovery trade-offs** explicit, including rollback risk and partial restoration.
Drive **post-incident** ownership, alerting, and architecture follow-ups.
exampleStories.weakVersion: I joined the incident bridge, helped debug, and sent updates whenever we learned something new.
followUpAngles: What did you communicate before **root cause** was known?

exampleStories.title: Security Token Exposure
exampleStories.promptVariant: Tell me about a time you led through a security or customer-trust crisis.
exampleStories.situation: An internal service exposed sensitive tokens in logs, and the team had to rotate credentials, assess **customer impact**, and decide notification scope.
strongAnswerSketch: Set up incident roles across Security, Engineering, Legal, Support, and Communications.
Prioritize containment and forensic evidence before broad speculation.
Communicate executive decisions around customer notification and risk posture.
Change logging standards, secret scanning, and production access reviews.
whyItWorks: Balances technical containment with trust and legal implications.
Turns the event into better controls.
exampleStories.weakVersion: We fixed the logging bug quickly, rotated tokens, and had Security handle the rest of the process.
followUpAngles: How did you decide customer notification scope?
What evidence did you need before communicating?

strongAnswerPattern.summary: The candidate shows operational discipline, communication clarity, accountability, and learning under pressure.
moves: Explains the command and communication structure.
Shows how decisions were made during incomplete information.
Avoids blame while still being rigorous.
Connects the crisis to lasting operational improvements.

weakAnswerPattern.summary: The candidate describes technical firefighting but misses leadership structure, communication, or learning.
redFlags: Centers the story on heroics rather than coordination.
Cannot explain who made decisions during the crisis.
Provides vague or defensive stakeholder communication.
The postmortem has no concrete follow-through.

followUps.question: Who was in command, and how were decisions made?
What did you communicate before you knew the **root cause**?
What **trade-offs** did you make during recovery?

signals.name: Calm Structure
signals.strong: Creates roles, decision paths, and update rhythms under pressure.
signals.weak: Lets the crisis run through ad hoc activity.

signals.name: Communication Clarity
signals.weak: Hides uncertainty or floods stakeholders with noise.

signals.name: Operational Learning
signals.strong: Turns crisis review into ownership, architecture, or monitoring changes.
signals.weak: Treats the review as a report-writing exercise.

rubric.expected: Leads team-level incidents with clear roles and follow-through.
Coordinates multi-team crises and communicates effectively across functions.
Manages organizational response, **executive communication**, customer impact, and systemic correction.
Owns company-level technology trust during crisis and changes risk governance afterward.

prompts.label: What crisis occurred, and what was at stake?
What response and communication responsibilities did you own?
How did you structure decisions, recovery, and updates?
What recovered, and what impact remained?
What did you learn about leading under pressure?

relatedScenarios: Handling customer trust damage after a data issue.
Communicating layoffs or a major reorganization with clarity and care.
